PAItMELEE (Shefford). Mr. Speaker, in rising to move concurrence in the third report of the Joint Committee of both Houses on the Printing of Parliament, I desire to make a brief explanation. Following a practice which has grown up, the committee ventured to recommend to this House the purchase of a certain number of copies of a book entitled ' Decisions of Speakers of the House of Commons.' The committee felt justified in taking that position, rely'ing upon the validity of the precedents which had been established in 1893, 1895, 1896 and 1898, when reports of a similar character had been concurred in by this House. My attention has been called to

631*

the constitutional aspect of a procedure of that kind. The committee is .prepared to assert all its rights and to exercise all the powers that are given to it ; but, on the other hand, it has no desire whatever to insidiously undermine the British constitution. It seems to me that when the committee makes a recommendation of this kind, and it is concurred in l>y the House, we strike at one of the fundamental principles of the constitution in respect to the appropriation of public moneys. It is a well known principle of the constitution that all appropriations of public funds and public revenues have to be initiated by the Crown and have to be brought down to this House by means of a message from His Excellency the Governor General. This question lias never been definitely settled, though at one time or another it has been brought up in this House. I would be very glad, as chairman of the committee, as I am sure all members of the committee would be, if this question were settled for all time to come on lines that would guide us as to our future action. There is no doubt that the Printing Committee has full power with respect to the printing of parliament, but I am not aware that any other powers are conferred on the committee. While on my feet, I might say that very often motions are made in this House to authorize the printing of parliamentary documents. Even that, I believe, is irregular, because I think that under the powers vested in the committee all motions respecting public and parliamentary printing should first be considered by that committee, and be brought before the House in the form of a report from us. In moving the adoption of the report, I have decided, for the reasons I have stated, to drop the particular clause recommending the purchase of books, which, logically, should be followed by an appropriation of money. I beg to move, seconded by Mr. Cowan :
That the third report of the Joint Committee of both Houses on the Printing of Parliament be concurred in, save and except the last paragraph, recommending the purchase of a book entitled ' Decisions of Speakers of the House of Commons.'
Motion agreed to.

House again in committee on Bill (No. 21) to amend and consolidate the laws respecting railways.-The Minister of Railways and Canals.
On section 227,
No train shall pass in or through any thickly peopled portion of any city, town or village, at a speed greater than six miles an hour, unless
the track is fenced in the manner prescribed by this Act.

I propose to amend this section, first by striking out the word 'six' and inserting the word 'ten'; second, by inserting after the word ' fenced ' the words 'or properly protected'; and, third, by adding at the end of the section the words ' unless permission is given by some regulation or order of the board, the board may limit such speed in any case to any rate which it deems expedient.'
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS (Hon. A. G. Blair).

speechtext:
I would ask the minister to explain exactly what is meant by these words ' or properly protected.' The old law from which this section is copied had not these words. I am afraid the section will be too wide to be much of a protection to the public upon the highway, if it is changed in the way proposed, unless we have something in the subsequent sections of the Act providing proper and adequate protection. The law as it is to-day allows no running at a higher rate than six miles an hour unless tlie track is properly fenced. I see that the minister is increasing that to ten miles an hour. Under the clause as the hon. minister proposes to amend it, even if the track is not fenced, the railways escape liability if the track is ' properly protected.' I do not know what that means, and I doubt very much whether the committee does ? I do not know any section of the Act providing for definite, proper protection on highway crossings. A great many different kinds of crossings may be made. But, in the earlier part of the Act, the minister told us that this would be made all right in the part we are now dealing with. We should have a definite, easily understood law, so that the people may know what their rights are throughout the Dominion at the ordinary highway crossings. We know that, if some town or thickly populated municipality goes to the expense and makes an appeal to the board, the board is likely to make some special order about it. But what about the ordinary highway crossing where the people have to go back and forward in pursuance of their ordinary avocation ? What is the protection there 1 What does this provide in the case of a farmer hauling his grain to market, making a proper use of the highway and meeting with an accident because a train is running at a speed greater than ten miles an hour ? Who is to say what his rights are ? There will be nothing in the Act to say what the protection should be. If we had the law as it is to-day it is easily interpreted, for everybody knows what proper fencing is, or. if not, he can find out. With all due deference to the hon. minister I think the way in which the law was first put before us is much better than it will be with the insertion of these words, ' or properly protected.' This Act requires the track to be fenced at million. Mr. PATERSON.	*
way crossings. Then, why not make them make the railways liable if they do not comply with the law. But if the amendment prevails, the railways will not be practically liable for accidents if they fail to comply with the law. The law will not be carried out, because nobody can know whether the track is ' properly protected ' or not. If this Act is going to provide that highway crossings must be fenced in a certain way, then the company ought to be responsible if they do not fence their tracks in that way. Before I sit down I would like to say that I do not think the words proposed to be added to the section ought to be accepted. If these words are adopted the effect will be that prima facie, the company are bound to protect these crossings in a certain way, yet, if the board chooses, it can give them permission to do otherwise. I do not think there ought to be one law for one township and another law for another; one law for one county and a different law for another county. I am against delegating to the board control of matters of this kind. I am as much in favour of the primary objects of the Bill-the appointing of a commission to deal with those matters that have been causing so much discussion in the country-as is the hon. minister or any other member of this House. But this is a matter that ought not to go to a commission, the power to say what should be the proper protection of ordinary crossings. The way it is now proposed, the board may fix the rate of speed over a crossing. I say that the ordinary evei'y day person in this country ought to know that is a proper rate of speed at an ordinary crossing, whether it is well protected or not, at which a train should run. Now, the minister proposes to let them out of the fencing in the manner prescribed by this Act, if they protect it in the manner prescribed by this Act. I do not know anything in this Act requiring any protection, and I am contending that either these words ' or protected as required by this Act ' should be' cut out, or else that there should be some well defined protection required at every crossing in the thickly populated parts of cities, towns and villages. The ordinary inhabitant as he comes to town and has to cross these tracks, is entitled to know what is the rate of speed at which trains are allowed to run, and this is allowed to be changed as now proposed, so that not only can the rate be as prescribed by this Act, which does not specifically describe it, but the power of fixing the rate is delegated to a commission. That must be what the minister has in his mind, that the board of commissioners are to settle what the rate of speed must be. Now, there should be a chance for the everyday man to know what the rates ire, he ought to have a right to see that this Act is carried out definitely and clearly in every place.
Do you not think the Sunday man ought to have that right as well as the everyday man ?

The everyday man goes out on Sunday. The hon. gentleman travels as much on Sunday as I do, and I think we are both everyday men. I think the hon. gentleman knows what I mean.
A man interested in the drainage which he brought up the other day is not able to come down to Ottawa and see these commissioners on every little matter that may require his attention, and which may be of importance to him though not to others. Now here is a section that is meant to be a guide, that is meant to be a prima facie rule. What dees it amount to '! How can any one tell what it means without invoking the aid of this commission ? I do not think this commission ought to have the power to say that in any village, city or town the trains should exceed a certain rate, notwithstanding that they are breaking the provisions of the Act that require certain protection in the way of fencing.
I think if we had the section put in this Bill as drawn by the minister originally, we would have a much better enactment.
I say that unless it can be improved upon, unless it c.m be shown to be unreasonable or unworkable, then that provision ought not to be amended. It would then read clearly and distinctly that they could not exceed ten miles an hour unless the track was fenced in the manner prescribed by the Act. That would be all that ought to prevail. If they can disregard thu fencing as required by tlie Act, and this Act does not require them to protect in any particular way, then make them responsible for it. The minister is proposing to delegate to the board power to limit such speed to any rate ^ which it deems expedient. He is undertaking to a \ it at not less than ten miles. I think it should be fixed so that the board cannot change it at their mere whim.

I did not think so much could be said upon the subject of these words ' or other protection.' It is a larger theme than I had imagined. I do not attach a great deal of importance to the words ' or other protection.' They were put in there because the fencing is not always possible, and fencing is not the only mode in which protection may be given. No trouble has ever arisen, but as a matter of fact there are places which require to be protected, and which are protected, without fencing, and it was thought well in going over the Bill again to enable them to provide other protection which the board should think sufficient and ample for the purpose. The hon. gentleman objects to such enormous power being given to'the board. Well, that is a very trifling power compared with many of the powers which are conferred upon the board. I am
not at all alarmed that the power will be abused in any shape or form. It is necessary that in all classes of this character there should be some elasticity, or if there cannot be elasticity under the Act itself, then some working tribunal should have the opportunity of saying when they should insist upon tiie outside limit or when they may modify or minimize that limit. When we had a little talk the other day about the rate of speed at which trains should run through cities and towns, two or three hon. gentlemen opposite suggested that the rate should be fixed and that the board should be given no right to limit the speed because railways run a great deal faster than they used to. The rate which we have fixed here is the rate which is allowed street railways to run on all streets in the cities of Canada, so far as I know. This rate can be run without any danger to the public, because that is not a minimum but a maximum speed. In the amendment which we propose here we are allowing the board to diminish that rate in any proper case. The hon. gentleman has argued as though the board were given by this section power to exceed that rate. That is not the fact, it is the other way. Now what harm is there in enabling the board, in a proper case, to reduce this limit of speed according to their judgment ?

speechtext: May I ask the hon. minister if there has been any general demand, for the amendment which the hon. minister proposes to increase the rate of speed at which trains may pass through any thickly peopled portion of any city, town or village from six miles an hour to ten miles an hour.

I have not heard of any general

demand. Considering the relative rates of speed and what they were when this six miles was first fixed I think ten miles an hour is not an unreasonable extension. Then we have the additional fact that with the appliances which are now available you can stop a train in fifty or sixty feet and sometimes in less than that, whereas, under the old method you could not stop a train in four or five times that distance.
No train shall pass in or through any thickly peopled portion of any city, town or village, at a speed greater than ten miles an hour, unless the track is fenced or properly protected in the manner prescribed by this Act.
The train may proceed through a thickly peopled part of a municipality at the rate of ten miles an hour, but it must not pass at a greater rate unless permission is afforded.

In the subsection which deals with the prevention of one train colliding with another, the Bill provides that a watchman should be there to give warning. You can just as well define what protection shall be afforded to foot passengers or vehicles using a crossing. I agree with my hon. friend that watchmen and gates are the proper protection. My experience is that where you have 100 accidents now, you would not have more than one if there was a watchman at the crossing. I do not believe that we should assume that this commission can decide what is proper protection any belter than the 214 members of this House. We come from all parts of the Dominion, and we know how the people live as well as this commission of three men can know ; we know what they are complaining of ; we are in touch with our constituents ; and we know what to do in regard to these unfortunate cases. People are killed too often by railway trains at these crossings, and the mere fact that the railway companies may have to pay some damages does not make it right. People do not want to have to run the risk, when they send their children to school, of having them killed, instead of coming home at night. We have inaugurated fast travel, and we are not thinking of the people who have to use the highways every day, and every minute of the day. If this Act is going to allow of a speed greater than has heretofore existed, we shall make no mistake in requiring railway companies to place watchmen at crossings in thickly populated portions of cities and towns. People talking together on the public highway, as they have a perfect right to do, might come to the track without hearing an approaching train. If a watchman were there, whose business would be to hold up his hand and stop those people by some sign, an accident would not occur ; and if the railroads are desirous of their trains travelling faster than

they have been and they are to be commended to a certain extent for doing that in the interests of the public-still they must not do it at the cost of human life. The only people who would object to this provision for a watchman would be the railway companies, on the score of expense. At these crossings they would have to employ a watchman at probably $1.50 a day-perhaps some men who lost a limb or been injured in their service, and whofti they ought to pension. In England, men who have lost an arm or a leg in the service of a railway company, instead of being pensioned, are usually employed as watchmen, in which capacity they do something to protect life and at the same time do something for their employers. If this section is allowed to stand until we come to the end of the Bill, and if the members of this House will study it, I think they will almost unanimously agree with me that the proper thing, instead of leaving the protection of life entirely to the board, will be for us to have the Act say ' unless a watchman is stationed at these crossings to give warning of the approach of trains.' We are better able to decide the matter ourselves than the board, and the railway companies ought not to complain if that is done.

The hon. Minister of Railways and Canals, in dealing with this section, and replying to the arguments advanced, tells us that in all cases there will be ample protection provided by the board. The hon. minister shakes his head, meaning that I am not right. I will, however, read the section :
Nto train shall pass in or through any thickly-peopled portion of any city, town or village, at a speed greater than ten miles an hour, unless the track is fenced or properly protected.
The minister says that the board will see to it that the track is fenced or is properly protected. As I am pointing out, this is a case in which the railway company desires to run their trains at a greater speed than ten miles an hour. They can do so if the track is fenced as prescribed by the Act, or is properly protected. In other words, the railway company do not need to come to tlie board to get permission to run twenty miles an hour, so long as the track is fenced as prescribed by the Act, or is otherwise properly protected. Leave the question of properly protected out of consideration for the moment. We have this state of facts, that if the railway company have their line fenced in the manner prescribed by the Act, they cam run just as fast as they like. The point we have to consider as a committee is this : is it wise or safe to give to the railway companies, without requiring them to come to the board at all, and without fencing their lines in the manner prescribed by the Act, the right to run in populous places at a speed greater than six miles an hour or up to ten miles an hour V The old Act said six miles an hour, li e are jumping from six miles to ten miles. Unless permission is given by some regulation or order of the hoard.
Now, what is the meaning of that ? It is not a case, mark you, of where the railway is properly protected or fenced. It is a case of where it is not properly fenced or protected. It is a case of where it is not fenced or protected at all. That is the sense of the section. If the railway is not fenced, the trains can run up to ten miles an hour ; and if the company come to the board in a case in which the track is not fenced or protected, the board can give them permission to run at any greater speed that the board think fit. That is the meaning of the section, and that is a power which it is not safe to give to any board or body of men without this parliament considering first, very carefully, what the result of that legislation will be. The minister has been arguing that the board will protect and will order the fence. That is not what we are dealing with. This is a case in which there is no fence or protection, and in which the board can give permission to run trains at any speed they think fit. Is that wise to do ? I am not going to repeat the arguments made by other hon. gentlemen on this side, but I want to add that, aside from these points, I am altogether in harmony with the proposition which has been enunciated so often, and do not want to confer on .any board any power which we can as safely and as well exercise ourselves.

My hon. friend is discussing this under a misapprehension. The only difference between this Bill and the existing law, either as regards fenced or unfenced localities or the control and regulation by this board and the Railway Committee of the Privy Council, is that we are giving a train, where the place is not properly fenced, the privilege of running ten miles an hour in place of six. speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: No, because if you struck them out the complainant would not get costs at all.
In Ontario costs will follow the event.
I do not think so.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: The person bringing tlie action might fail because of the indulgence given to the company, but he ought to get his costs because he is justified in laying the information. Therefore, I think the hon. member for Yale and Cariboo is quite right in saying that costs should be within the discretion of the court.
I am quite agreeable to the question of costs being left in the discretion of the court.

speechtext: Strike out the words ' but witii costs in any event against the company ' and insert in lieu thereof ' and costs shall be in the discretion of the court.
That subsection two be amended by striking out the words ' but with costs in any event against the company ' and inserting in lieu thereof ' and coats shall be in the discretion of thle court.'

speechtext: I would rather strike the whole section out than say as the present Bill says, that the cost shall be in any event against the company.

speechtext: I do not know but that the suggestion of the hon. member for Yale and Cariboo (Mr. Galliher) is a good one. The question of cost should be left to the discretion of the court. I would like to know what the hon. minister thinks about it. I do not think it should be struck out and left in such a position that the party making the complaint should get no costs where his action was shown to be justifiable. If it is left within the discretion of the court then, it is merely a matter of spite on the part of the person bringing the action, the court will not give him his costs, but if it is shown that his action is justifiable and if it is found that the obstruction is excusable, then the court will give costs to the complainant.

Does the hon. gentleman agree with the suggestion of the hon. member for Yale and Cariboo, that it ought to be left in the discretion of the court ?
Section, as amended, agreed to.
On section 224,
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext:
I was not in the House when section 224 of this Bill was considered, and I desire to call the attention of the minister to a matter which, I think, ought to be provided for by that section. This section provides :
The bell with which the engine is furnished shall be rung, or (except within the limits of cities or incorporated towns) the whistle sounded, at the distance of at least eighty rods from every place at which the railway crosses or is carried along any highway, and be kept ringing, or except as aforesaid, he sounded at short intervals, until the engine has crossed such highway.
In towns or cities or villages where railways pass, very frequently two and perhaps three, and in a case I know of four streets are crossed by the railway within a distance of eighty rods. I had occasion to try a case last fall with the Bay of Quinte Railway in which the court had to construe the section of the old Act which is similar to this. Iin that particular case the railway started from the Rathbun Company's works and before it reached what is known as the Kingston road, it had to

cross diagonally four streets in the town. Leaving the Rathbun Company's works the whistle was sounded and they kept on ringing the bell and sounding the whistle until the engine had crossed the first street. That sounding of the whistle and that ringing of the bell was all within eighty roads of the Kingston road, but they ceased blowing the whistle and ceased ringing the bell after the engine had crossed the first street and they contended before the court that under this section they were not obliged to sound the whistle or ring the bell after crossing the first street it being within eighty rods of the Kingston road. A person passing on the Kingston road was struck by the train and seriously iujured, his horse killed and his wagon demolished. The case was tried before Sir John Boyd and he held that the railway company having sounded the whistle and having rung the bell until the engine had crossed the first highway they had complied with the section o'f the statute, and they were not obliged to sound the whistle or ring the bell when crossing the intermediate streets, they being within eighty rods of the first crossing. It seemed to me to be a very hard ruling, but nevertheless the case was argued as ably as I could, and that was the decision. This *being the construction placed upon the-law by the courts, it appears to me that this clause should be amended so as to obviate such a ruling in future. I invite the attention of the minister to the matter.
Did the hou. gentleman appeal the case ?
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: I did not appeal the case. I had no occasion to appeal it because the case went to the jury. The judge found that there was sufficient evidence to send the ease to the jury and the jury beat the judge.
Hear, hear.

But in the judge's charge, he charged the jury that the company had performed its whole duty; the jury took the opposite view and held that the railway company had not performed its duty. They gave a verdict against the railway company and the railway company did not see fit to appeal. I would suggest that this section should be so amended as to compel the railway to sound the bell at every crossing.
That is what it means.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: That is what is intended no doubt, but the opposite construction was placed upon it by the court.
By the judge ; the jury set him right.

I do not see how it could possi-Mr. PORTER.
bly admit of such an interpretation ; I do not think you could use any language that could be clearer.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: Stress was laid by the court on the expression ' and to be kept ringing until the engine has crossed such highway.'
That means every highway.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: That was my contention and the judge said, no.
Would it be held that this provision of the Act is complied with if a train started to go one hundred miles and rang tlie bell before starting, and not afterwards?
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: That was not the holding. It was that if the whistle was sounded, eighty' rods from the first highway it need not be sounded again on a highway within that eighty rods.

Would the minister be kind enough to point out to me where in this Bill the public are protected against a careless engineer who runs a train backward and forward on a crossing for say half an hour ? I know of a case where the public are delayed almost every day from fifteen minutes to half an hour by the shunting of cars across a highway.
On what railway ?
The Dominion Coal Company's Railway, and the Intercolonial Railway.
This Bill does not apply to the Intercolonial Railway.
It applies to the Dominion Coal Company's lime.
The Intercolonial Railway is one of the worst offenders in that respect. I have known them to hold up traffic at a crossing for nearly half an hour.
I am afraid that my hon. friend has a very sharp eye for any little sins of omission or commission on the Intercolonial Railway.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: I do not think the minister is justified in saying that, because I have criticised the Intercolonial Railway very little since I have been in this House.
Not half as much as it deserved.
Not half as much as it deserved.
Not half as much as you think you might, I suppose.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext:
Perhaps not half as much as I might in justice. I have suffered in

the same way as the hon. member for Cape Breton, and I trust that the minister will, through his employees prevent that in future.

There is no doubt that the employees are very often at fault. I do not see how you can stop engines from going backward and forward on highways as long as highways and trains exist. We provide that a train shall not stand at a crossing for longer than five minutes at one time, and that is not unreasonable.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: That does not meet the case.
I suppose the only way to meet the case would be to stop the railway.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: The station agent should be empowered to insist that the man on the locomotive should make reasonable provision for the passage of the traffic which accumulates at crossings. Again and again I have seen a number of vehicles stopped for half an hour while these cars were being shunted backward and forward. Provision should be made to prevent that.

I will give the minister a case in point, where there ought to be a better regulation of the running of trains. There is a crossing in my constituency which is just at the exit of the Grand Trunk yard at East -Toronto village. All the shunting tracks there converge on the main line, and the sorting of freight trains takes place. This is done so rapidly, the trains running backward and forward at intervals of only a few seconds, that there is no chance for vehicles to cross. I have seen from twelve to twenty vehicles stopped at that particular point and prevented from crossing by this shunting. The board ought to have power to compel these trains to check up, say every second time, long enough to allow vehicles to cross.
The board has that power.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: This section of the Bill will not meet the case brought forward by the hon. member for Cape Breton (Mr. Kendall), because it does not apply to the Intercolonial Railway at all, and we who live along the line of that railway will have no redress in case of traffic being obstructed.
You will be able to get at it more easily than through the board.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: It does not have much effect, though.
Does the minister believe that it will be easier to bring the Intercolonial Railway to time than the railways controlled by this board ?
Yes.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: Then I think he is fortifying the argument of the hon. gentlemen on this side against clothing the board with all these powers.

It might be easy for the hon. member for Cape Breton and those who think with him politically to bring the Intercolonial Railway to time, but the members on this side of the House may not find it so easy until we have a change of government.
Will the minister tell me what _ clause protects the public in case of shunting ?
Section 229.

That does not do it at all. That refers to a train standing on a crossing. There are ten tracks at the point I refer to, and if you get across one you are pocketed among the others. The trains keep going up aud down the different tracks and completely block the traffic. I have been held at that crossing for over half an hour. The Bill does not protect the public in a case of that kind. I ask the minister to put in a small clause giving the board power to make a regulation to meet such a case.

I think we might insert, in section 229, at the end of the first clause, these words :
Or by so using the tracks in the shunting as to obstruct public traffic for a longer period than three minutes at one time.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: I scarcely think that meets the objection. They might obstruct the traffic for three minutes and then, after the intermission of a minute, obstruct it again.
They must allow the traffic to get across. If they do not allow sufficient time for the traffic to get across, they are obstructing.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext:
Amendment agreed to.
On section 233-telegraphs and telephones,

In connection with sections 233 and 234, I think there should be a clause of this kind :
The company shall, subject to the approval of the board, grant equal telephone entrance to its stations to all individuals or telephone companies asking therefor. For every case of violation of this section, the servant or agent who has charge of the station is liable on a summary conviction to a fine of $100, and the company is also liable for such violation to a fine of $500. Any contract between the company and a telephone company or individual for exclusive telephone entrance to a station is declared to bo Illegal.
I am now bringing up a question which is a substantial grievance existing ail over this



country to-day. It is a fact that the Grand Trunk, the Canadian Pacific and the Canadian Northern companies have entered into contracts with the Bell Telephone Company, whereby that company has an exclusive entrance into all the stations of these three great railways. The result is that if a municipality establishes a telephone system, as the two thriving towns of Port Arthur and Fort William have done, or if the farmers of any locality, when they cannot get a satisfactory service from the Bell Telephone Company, establish a telephone service of their own, they are denied entrance to the railway stations of these railways. I say that should not be, but the railway companies should be compelled to give a telephone entrance to their stations to all persons applying for it on equal terms. In the township of Markham, in my constituency, and in the adjoining township of Pickering, in West Ontario, the farmers for a long time wanted telephone communication, and could not get it from the Bell Telephone Company. At last eighteen farmers and storekeepers in that neighbourhood united and established their own telephone system. Every one of them was a good customer of the Canadian Pacific Railway, travelled over it and gave it their freight ; and when they established this private telephone line and asked for a connection with the Locust Hill station of the Canadian Pacific Railway, they were told that they could not have it, that the agreement to which I have referred precluded it. The result is that these people cannot have telephone access to the station to ask whether the train is on time, whether their freight has arrived, or any other question in connection with the traffic of the railway.
The agreement to which I have referred is against public policy. I consulted eminent counsel and obtained the opinion that it was illegal. I had the company indicted before the grand jury, bat the judge held that it was doubtful whether the charge held or not, and instructed the grand jury to dismiss the case, or have the indictment drawn in a different way. If that be the case, surely the law ought to be amended. Let me state another instance, and I am sorry that the bon. member for Algoma (Mr. Dyment) is not here to back me up. The two thriving towns of Port Arthur and Fort William established a very satisfactory telephone system, owned by the municipalities, on the same lines as those followed by municipalities in Great Britain, yet although these two towns are on the line of the Canadian Pacific Railway, and do almost all their business with that railway, they are deprived of telephone access to the two stations in these places. That has occurred more or less all over Canada, and if we are to encourage the establishment of municipal telephone systems in this country, the law must be changed and the farmers in the municipalities must be given access Mr. MACLEAN.
to the railway station for telephone purposes. There is nothing of so much importance to the farming community to-day as the establishment of rural telephones. It has done a great deal in the United States to make life on the farm interesting and enjoyable, but if these people, who are forcing the monopoly to cut down its rates, are not to be allowed to bring their lines into the railway stations, they will not be able to do business. Half the telephone business of the farmers has to do with questions of freight, and the farmers can only get the information they desire by having free access to the railway stations. I have heard it argued in this House that this would interfere with the management of railways, because it would take up too much of the time of the station agent, and interfere with his other duties, but he need not answer the telephone at all unless when he is doing nothing else. Besides any man is free to go into a station and ask about his goods and the arrival and departure of trains, and why should he not have equal liberty to put these questions through a telephone ? There is nothing unfair in this, and in any ease surely the railway company is in a position to employ a boy or girl to answer these telephone calls. The other day I heard a gentleman say, in discussing this question, not very far from here, that if any attempt were made in the west to prevent the farmers having access with their telephones to railway stations, there would soon be cutting of wires. Well, when the telephone system is extended to that country, not a single line except the Bell Telephone Company will have access to the railway stations. Is it right that these railway companies, which have obtained enormous franchises from this country, should discriminate against any body who wants telephone access to their stations ? It is not in the interests of the farmers, it is not in the interests of the people who have given these railway companies immense subsidies and franchises.
It is questionable if it is in the interest of the railway companies.

It is not in the interest of the railway companies themselves. As I pointed out in a telegram I sent to Sir Thomas Sliaughnessey, surely you do not intend to treat in this way the people wTho are your best customers, who furnish traffic to your road, and who are simply asking the privilege of telephone access to your station. To-day there are private lines waiting the decision of parliament on this question.
Do you want every private line to have access to the railway stations ?

1 have made it subject to the approval of the board. If you build a line to the station and wish to speak over

it to the railway agent, to ask about your freight, why should you not be free to do so 1 A man can make the inquiry by entering the door, why should he not be allowed to speak through a hole in the wall, when it can be done so much more expeditiously.
But do not have it a private line.
Well, the Bell line is a private line. I do not see how else you can define it.
Oh, no.
It is a line owned by a private corporation.
For the use of the public.

But a private line should have as much right as a corporation line with regard to access to a railway station. Let the hon. gentleman (Mr. Galli-her) suggest bow it can be done otherwise than it is done here. All I want is not to discriminate against one line in favour of another. I want this nefarious agreement between the Canad an Pacific and the Grant Trunk and the Bell Telephone Company declared to be against public policy. In my Bill I propose to provide that aiiy contract between a telephone company and a railway company giving exclusive access to the railway station, be declared illegal. And it ought to be declared illegal in the interest of the farming community and the business community', and for the general progress of the country. Nothing will do so much for the country as the cheapening of telephone communication. And here is this agreement made last year. Representatives of the company have said it is only a renewal of a former agreement. And the Bell Telephone Company got a year's grace from this parliament last year, and the Minister of Justice gave a pledge to the people of the country that he would bring in a law regulating the operation of the telephone companies, but so far, that law is not forthcoming. I have introduced a Bill of that kind, which is now before a sub-committee. I do not know that it will ever reach the House. But, now that the bon. minister has brought in a Bill dealing with railways, and now that we are considering the clause dealing with telegraphs and telephones, I appeal to the minister to take my suggestion and incorporate in his Bill this clause, or a clause having a similar effect.

I notice that in these clauses relating to telegraphs and telephones, the position of the government is satisfactorily guarded. The government may have the exclusive use of telephone and telegraph lines, and the government may erect telegraph or telephone lines on the rail-1CS1
way's right of way. But since these sections were formed, a new element has sprung up in the country. That element is the telephone business. The telephone is extending throughout all the country districts. The matter which the hon. member for East York (Mr. Maclean) speaks of was a very live question in the riding next to mine last season. But the matter the hon. gentleman speaks of, the agreement between the railway companies and the telephone companies, was of such a nature that it precluded the farmers from obtaining connection with the railway station by their own independent line of telephone. Now, I seriously think that, as the telephone is to be such an important factor in our home life, we should see to it that me rights of the people in it are carefully guarded. I cannot see, for my part, why an independent telephone line should not have communication with the railway station. In many places throughout this country the railway station is practically the centre of the district. It is there the goods are carried to and it is from there the goods are taken ; and the communication of the people seems to be naturally with the railway station. And, the people being accustomed to the use of the telephone, I cannot see any difference between a person calling up the railway station by telephone and one going in at the door to ask a question of the station master. However, if it is thought to be too great a hardship to place upon the agent at the station the duty of answering the telephone, why not allow an arrangement whereby' an independent line or lines could keep an operator there for their one purpose '! Some arrangement of that kind should be made in the interests of the public. I have been thinking over the telephone business of the country, and 1 am not sure that the government should not own the trunk telephone lines and allow anybody to communicate over them who desires to do so. That is a question, of course, which will come up in the future. But we have telephone lines widely in use now, and the use is rapidly extending, it is a cheap means of communication as it is now carried on. In the western states, I am told, the farmers, even use the top wire of their fences for telephoning, and when they come to a highway crossing, they simply elevate the wire. It offers a very convenient way for the farmers to communicate with one another. Of course, it is not suitable for long distances, but, over short distances it works very well. There is no doubt that the telephone is with us to stay, and it is bound to be the medium of communication for the people.. Any law that interferes with the rights of the people in the use of the telephone matter, should be cancelled.

There is a point to which the attention of the government should be drawn, but which I have not heard men-

tinned so far. I am in the electric business and am planting poles about the streets of our town and know the difficulties we have to contend with, both with the people and also with the telephone and telegraph companies. We have gone to a great deal of expense in our town improving our streets, putting down nice boulevards, macadamizing the roads, laying concrete sidewalks, and generally trying to improve and beautify the town in every way. And it is most objectionable to have the telegraph company plant hideous poles wherever they see lit, not painted, but covered over with all kinds of notices, advertisements of patent medicines and so on. Something should be done to compel these people to put up uniform poles and paint them, and also to prevent them planting them where they are objectionable to the people. We paint our poles, but the telegraph people refuse to do so. These poles are an eyesore on our most travelled thoroughfare. We think that something should be done to bring these poles under the control of the government or somebody so that these people may be obliged to make these poles look as respectable as they can be made, and also to place them where they will be least objectionable. We think also that it is not necessary that the telegraph poles should be on the principal street of the town. We do not object to the ffeleplione poles, because they are used by every one. But the telegraph poles can just as well be put on the back streets. As to the main line leading to the office, which naturally *would be on a main street, we would not object to the poles. But, except for this, there is no reason why they should occupy the most prominent place in our town.

This discussion impresses upon me the necessity of the government taking a step in advance, as has been done in other countries. In New South Wales, the telephone system throughout that whole state, including the city of Sydney, with a population much larger than that of any city of the Dominion, is owned by the government. In New Zealand, the government owns the telegraphs, and they also own then- railways, and that is something that we also should have in the interest of the people of the Dominion.

While I agree with much that is in the motion of the hon. member for East York, I think that some of its provisions are rather drastic. I do not know that I should go so far as to enact a flue against the operator in case he refused to answer the telephone. It seems to me they would obey the law without a penalty. I suppose, however, you could hardly have a law without a penalty, ' but it struck me, as I listened to the amendment that the penalty seemed rather hard upon the operator, and, perhaps, upon the company.

I have made this amendment on the lines of section 229, where there is a clause for a penalty in case of violation. I do not insist on the large sum of $50 and $500, if there is some kind of penalty. But I want to say in the last clause that any existing contracts of this nature are declared illegal. Now, I may be told that I will be interfering with existing rights. But as a matter of fact this contract is felt by the railway companies to be so bad that they have put into it a clause themselves w'hick will enable them to cancel it. I believe, Sir Thomas Shaughnessy is ashamed of it to-day, and is only waiting for an opportunity to cancel it, because it is so unfair towards the people wdio patronize his road. So if it is urged that to declare this contract illegal would interfere with any vested rights, I have only to say that the companies themselves have guarded themselves by inserting a clause that they can declare it off. While I am on my feet, I wish also to point out that in many places where these independent lines have been started, there is no Bell Telephone Company there, and yet the Bell Telephone Company debars independent lines from coming into the stations. These telephone lines run several miles from the railroad stations, to little centres twelve miles from the stations, where store-keepers, farmers and drovers wish to be in communication with the station, but they cannot get access to that station by reason of the agreement with the Bell Telephone Company. If that be the case, surely in all justice we ought to give these drovers, these farmers, and these traders, a right to use an independent telephone line in obtaining information from the railway stations.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Is this amendment a subsection or is it an amendment to the section ?
I will leave that to the minister to determine.
The hon. gentleman proposes, I understand, to provide a penalty as a subclause to 234.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: In addition to (B) which deals with telegraph and telephones, in any *way the hon. gentleman likes.
That is certainly not germane to the subjects referred to in either of the two sections.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: It is germane to telephones.
I do not see how it would be a subclause to either of the other two.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: I did not say a subclause, it is to amend the section coming under B, which deals with telegraphs and telephones.

I am not going to deal with that, that is a private motion. The question arises whether this committee is ready to adopt such a proposition as the hon. gentleman has made. I am compelled to state to the committee what I think are objections to it. I think it would disfigure the whole Bill if we were to add to it a clause of this character. The hon. gentleman proposes that * subject to the approval of the board, the railway company shall grant equal telephone entrance to its stations to all individuals or telephone companies asking therefor.' Now, is that not a very serious proposition, that railway companies shall grant equal telephone entrance to all telephone companies and to all individuals V In the first place, the suggestion that any individual may claim the privilege of using the railway company's offices for this purpose, is so extreme and so indefensible a proposition, that I do not think it requires to be thought over very much.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: Does the hon. gentleman recollect that all this is subject to the approval of his own board, which has his confidence ?

I trust the parliament of Canada is not going to put upon record any declaration that the board will have to consider and determine whether individuals shall have the right to claim entrance to the stations of railroad companies. It is an utterly absurd proposition, it is entirely in violation of all principle. What right has this parliament to say that A, B, C and D may take possession of the property of a railway company, or of the accommodation which a railway company affords in their business, that telephone companies may come in and use their property, ' free gratis for nothing,' heat, light, room, wall (space, accommodation, all for nothing ? What kind of a proposition is that ? It is not merely socialistic, it is confiscatory. You incorporate a railway compa ny for the purpose of conducting a railway business; what right have you to say that they shall be under compulsion to allow their offices to be used by anybody that a telephone company may want to send there for the purpose of tendering a telephone message, that they shall provide wall space for that telephone, office room for a clerk or agent, that they shall bear out of their own pockets the expense ? The telephone company is a prosperous institution, it is a uesful and Important institution, and necessary for the business of the country, contributory to the success and prosperity of the country; but are you going to allow it to call upon the railway company to pay the expense
of the telephone company doing its own business ? Now, the hon. gentleman does not seriously mean to ask this committee to consider a proposition of that kind.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: I never was more serious in my life, but I do not think the hop. gentleman is.
If one individual, then 15,000 or 20,000 may be allowed the same privilege.

I think it would be unfair to limit it to 20,000. I think the hon. gentleman would not be satisfied with less than 100,000. What I think would solve the whole problem, without taking anybody's property or time, or imposing any duties upon anybody else, which they do not want to assume from a business point of view, would be to permit somebody living in the immediate locality, in the neighbourhood of the station-as the hon. gentleman said, these stations are generally in populous towns, somewhere near the centre of the town-let the telephone company have a telephone in some place handy to the station, and when somebody wants to do business, let him go into the office and pay the agent for doing it, pay as they ought to pay. That would be a reasonable suggestion, and there would be no occasion then for confiscating anybody's property. There is no limit. I do not know where my hon. friend would stop in his socialistic legislation. The word ' radical ' does not begin to express it.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: Go on, go on.
And then does any one but my hon. friend suppose that a contract or agreement which has been made between a telephone company and a railway is illegal ?
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: An agreement against public policy ?
Against public policy ?
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: Yes.
My hon. friend is to be the final tribunal to determine what public policy is.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: As much as the hon. gentleman is.
My hon. friend is not willing to have anybody but himself have an opinion on this subject.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: Yes, he is.

He is not willing to admit that there is any room to doubt the reasonableness of his opinion and he is going to ask parliament to declare that a binding contract made under the law is illegal. My hon. friend tells us that the Canadian Pacific

Railway themselves are ashamed of the contract they made with the Bell Telephone Company. My hon. friend no doubt has communicated with the president of the Canadian Pacific Railway and has been informed that such is the case because he would not say so if he did not believe it. If they are ashamed why do they not seek for some mode of escape ? Under a clause of this contract that my hon. friend wants this parliament to declare to be illegal when it is illegal, provision .is made that by notice either party may terminate the agreement. This shameful agreement which the Canadian Pacific Railway admittedly avow is one that they are ashamed of has a clause which will enable them to terminate it. Terminate it and it is all over and you do not need to ask parliament to discredit itself by assuming to declare that a contract which is valid and legal is illegal. My hon. friend, with his extreme, radical ideas, says that this is against public policy. There is no reason for such legislation at all. These people can proceed upon a business basis, pay their money like men, have somebody at hand at the station to go in and get the information they want and answer their -calls. My hon. friend asserts that the machinery of a great parliament shall be employed in doing something which it would only be justified in doing under the most extreme circumstances. My hon. friend has told us the remedy. It is at hand and these people can employ it at any time they please. I shall trust that parliament will not feel called upon to proceed any further with the consideration of the amendment proposed by my hon. friend.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I have had a good deal of this kind of badinage from the hon. Minister of Railways and Canals in connection with these propositions which I have introduced into this House, but I intend to follow him and to meet him on this question before the people of Ontario. He will have to settle with his supporters from Ontario for what he lias said here to-day, and the right hon. Prime Minister (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) will have to settle with the people of Ontario for the nonsense that the hon. minster has spoken here to-day. The hon. gentleman has spoken as the attorney of the telephone companies, as a holder of telephone stock, and not as Minister of Railways and Canals, protecting public interests. He says that such a proposition as this disgraces the Bill. Let me read section 278 of the hon. gentleman's Bill :
Every company which grants any facilities for the carriage of goods by express to any incorporated express company or person, shall grant equal facilities, on equal terms and conditions, to any other incorporated express company which demands the same.
Is that socialistic ? Is that radical ? Is that allowing equal terms to all ? What he Hon. Mr. BLAIR.
said of me he said of his own Bill. Has he any explanation to offer to the committee ? Has he any excuse to offer to the committee or to the farmers of this country for this socialistic, this confiscatory legislation ? He uses the latest Oxford and Cambridge accent of the word ' confiscatory,' and I agree with him in that.
I am glad that the hon. gentleman agrees with me in something.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: That the way for these people to do, the hon. minister says, is to put a telephone in some house adjoining the sation and get somebody from the station to attend to it. The way the answers are got to-day is through the Bell Telephone Company having a telephone in every station in this country. The railway companies are only too glad to allow them in, to give wall space and to give the necessary service to answer the calls. But by reason of this contract they say that no one else shall get in. The Grand Trunk Railway, Canadian Pacific Railway and Canadian Northern are allowed free telephones in consideration of that concession. They all get something for the exclusive use of the stations, but they get it at the expense of their own customers. If the people of Canada, who want this question of telephone service settled, insist upon their representatives in this House voting for this socialistic proposition, this radical proposition, they will get what they want and the question will be settled in the public interest. I would like the hon. Minister of Railways and Canals to go to any place in the county of York and talk as he has talked here to-day, or, I would like the right hon. Prime Minister to go with his entourage, including the hon. Minister of Railways and Canals, and speak in the same manner as the hon. minister has spoken here to-day.
I wTould not be the least bit afraid to.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext:
We will meet the hon. minister there. He has asked his followers to throw this reasonable proposition out. I have brought it forward in a reasonable way, I have based it on a clause already in the Bill, I have done it in the public interest. I do not think it is socialistic, but I think it is right. Such legislation is demanded by the country to-day. Are the farmers of Canada not to have the same privileges that the farmers of the United States enjoy ? The people in the North-west Territories are rising to the importance of having telephone lines all through the west and we are inviting immigrants to come and settle upon our western lands. Are we to tell them that they are not to be treated in the same way as they are treated in Europe in regard to telephones ? Does the right hon. leader of

the government not know that in Europe, in Norway and Sweden, in Germany and elsewhere, where the people own their telephones, everybody has the right of access to the railway station to telephone and inquire as to the shipment of his goods. Moreover, they have their telephone for eight, ten and twelve dollars a year, while the Bell Telephone Company?* which is protected by the hon. Minister of Railways and Canals, is charging the people of Canada $25, $30, $40, $50, $00, and up to $100 a year for a similar service. I pay $175 a year for my telephone service.
It is cheap at that.

It is cheap at that and I can pay it. But, I have neighbours who cannot pay it. I know a gentleman living six miles out of the city who implored the Bell Telephone Company to give him telephone connection. Doctors, who are subject to call at all hours of the night are unable to secure a telephone service. My neighbour is a veterinary surgeon and horses are driven from five to twenty miles every night to his place by people who want him to go out and attend to their sick cattle. He cannot get telephone connection for less than $150 a year. This may be a radical proposition, it may be a socialistic proposition, but it deals with a crying grievance all over this country and that grievance is the attitude of the Bell Telephone Company towards the people. It is manifestly opportune to introduce this subject in connection with the railway law which is before the House, but the hon. Minister of Railways and Canals says that to do something in the interests of the people who transact business with railways is socialistic and confiscatory. I do not agree with him and I do not think hon. gentlemen opposite agree with the attitude of the hon. minister. I have had conversations with a great many of them and I have had letters from a great many people on this subject. I have spent a good deal of time in dealing with this question. In dealing with this question before a special committee not far away from here I have had paid lawyers of the Bell Telephone Company holding me up day after day and not allowing me to make any progress. I may not be able to make any progress here, but there is a higher court in this country, the court of the people. The people are thinking about this condition of affairs and I am going to talk to the people all over the province of Ontario. I am just beginning a career in connection with it. I do not know whether it will amount to much or little, but I am going to the people of Ontario to discuss this question with them. I have discussed it in the press and I have had a certain amount of recognition, but I am going on the stump if there is an
election coming on and I want to meet the hon. Minister of Railways and Canals on the stump in Ontario, and hear him tell the people that legislation dealing with these telephone companies and compelling a railway company to give equal terms to all telephone organizations is bad legislation, is radical legislation, and is disfiguring his Bill. Is not his Bill disfigured by some other things ? I am not disfiguring his Bill.
I am giving him credit for his Bill. I am giving the minister credit that he is attempting for the first time to give a broad general Act dealing with the railway question. I congratulate the Prime Minister and his colleagues on having the courage to bring in a Bill of this kind and I am willing to help them to perfect it.
Hear, hear.

In no way have I tried to block that Bill. I am only trying to help them perfect it in the interests of the people. But, because I am doing that, I am told I am doing something socialistic, and something against public policy. Well, I am not. I tell the Minister of Railways and Canals that if he persists in the attitude he has taken here to-day, all I want is to meet him in the province of Ontario. I want him to ccme to Locust Hill in the township of Markham, in my county where there is a Liberal majority of 300 and if they do not knock that township out of my county-1 can meet the Minister of Railways and Canals in that township and I can knock that 300 Liberal majority to smithereens on that one question alone.
Hear, hear.
I hope my lion.' friend (Mr. Maclean) will not insist on this challenge until after the session.

This gives the provisional directors all the powers of permanent directors.
What Is the object of this company ?

To erect elevators at Port Coiborne and put on a line of boats to carry grain from Port Coiborne to Montreal, and also from the upper lakes down to Port Coiborne. The intention is to transport the products of the North-west down through the St. Lawrence canals to Montreal. It Is impossible for steamers that come down the upper lakes to- pass through the canals, as they draw from eighteen to twenty feet of

How will this affect the improvements which the Minister of Public Works contemplates making to the harbour at Port Colborne ?

The government, I understand, have deepened Port Colborne harbour to twenty or twenty-two feet, and have built a breakwater to protect the harbour from the storms on the lake. This company is asking for power to erect elevators and put on steamers to carry the grain down to Montreal.

The objectionable part is that you are giving to the provisional directors the power of collecting money, depositing it in bank and taking it out and using it, without being elected. These are powers we never give provisional directors, and I see no reason why we should do so in this case.

Mr? REII) (Grenville). Then, the position has been finally filled ? In filling it by the appointment of Mr. Keilty who is a very capable man was it filled in accordance with the Civil Service Act ?

That is not my opinion.

In this case the hon. minister has filled the position in this way :	When Mr. Keilty was appointed he
said that he would simply appoint him deputy collector without requiring him to pass an examination of any kind. If a gentleman who is appointed deputy collector is allowed to keep the office open for a year, as in this case, and passes a simple promotion examination he can be appointed collector of the port. No, I think the hon. gentleman is mistaken altogether. First, Mr. Keilty was appointed an exciseman. After having passed the promotion examination as a third class officer he was appointed to the position of deputy collector and from that position to the position of collector.

The hon. minister knows that in that town if you have a collector you only require one deputy collector, and the hon. minister knows he got around the appointing of an excise man by appointing another deputy collector. Therefore, in that town he has two deputy collectors, and a collector. In that way the hon. minister got around the law in regard to the qualifications necessary for appointing an excise mail. I would like to know if the work done in Prescott calls for the appointment of a second deputy collector ?

If there was a violation of the law it was violated the next day after it was passed. It has been the habit of the department since the law was passed to appoint deputy collectors belonging to Class A or Class B and according to the law no examination is required for either one or the other. This practice has been followed both by the present government and its predecessor and therefore there has been no new departure. This has been done since the law was enacted over 20 years ago. This is not the only place where deputy collectors are appointed. We have them in Montreal, Toronto, Windsor, Belleville and many other places ; in fact, this is the only available position for those who have not passed their examination. My own opinion is that this does not

*entitle gentlemen to be promoted to the position of collector unless they have qualified themselves afterwards, either by passing the qualifying examination or the promotion examination.

What I mean is this. In the town of Prescott, when the position of exciseman became vacant, the Civil Service Act required the minister to appoint a person who had passed the qualifying examination, and in order to get around that he appointed to the position of deputy collector a man who had never passed the civil service examination at all.
That is the law.

I admit that. You can appoint him as deputy collector, but you immediately sent that gentleman out to fill the position of exciseman. That is overriding the Civil Service Act in every shape and form. Is not that a fact ?

If it is a fact, then it has been overridden hundreds of times. I have said that an exciseman is sometimes appointed temporarily until the examination takes place. If a man is to be appointed a deputy collector, neither qualifying nor promotion examination is required, but sometimes after they pass their [DOT]examination they prefer to be appointed excisemen and then go up for their promotion [DOT]examination. The only position open to those who have not passed their examination is that of deputy collector. We have done, and all governments have done the same thing, in appointing a man temporarily until the examination takes place.
I understand all that very well, but the minister is trying to get around the thing in hardly a fair way.
Not at all.

According to the minister's statement the deputy collector should have passed the promotion examination before he became collector. The minister has appointed another deputy collector since, and he therefore has a deputy collector there who has not passed the civil service examination, and who is filling the duties of exciseman.
Yes.

And the minister says that the appointment is made temporarily in order to give him a chance to qualify at the next civil service examination. If the law allows you to appoint a deputy collector who will fill the position of exciseman, then what is the good of the Civil Service Act in that respect ?

I -wish to be perfectly understood, and I think I know something about the law. Mr. Keilty was promoted to the position of deputy collector after having passed the promotion examination. From that position he was raised to the position of collector. The only position in the excise service to which a person can be appointed without examination is that of deputy collector, and it has always been the custom in the department to appoint an exciseman temporarily until he could have an opportunity to pass the examination. There is nothing in the law which prevents a man who has passed his promotion examination, and has been an exciseman, to be appointed a deputy collector arid then a collector, if the government wishes to appoint him. As the bon. member for Victoria (Hon. Mr. Costigan) has explained, there is the qualifying examination fixed by law and there, is the promotion examination governed by the regulations of the department. I am not objecting.
He was appointed because he was qualified according to the law, having passed, not the qualifying examination, but the promotion examination, which entitled him to a higher rank in the service.

The hon. gentleman does not seem yet to understand the question I asked, because he has not given me any answer whatever. I asked him if the position of exciseman required certain qualifications, or if candidates for that position had to pass a certain examination. Then I asked why he appointed a man in the town of Prescott who had never passed the civil service examination, and allowed him to act as an exciseman.

There could be no objection to the appointment or promotion of Mr. Keilty. There was another man appointed in Prescott, Mr. White; he never passed any examination. He was appointed deputy collector. But when a man is appointed to any position, whatever may be the name of it, whether collector, deputy collector, exciseman, or any other, the duties he has to perform are assigned to him by his superior officer. The fact that a man is an exciseman does not imply that he is to be confined to the duties of an exciseman. The work is distributed by the collector or other superior officer, and the deputy collector may fulfil the duties of an exciseman.

The hon. minister has now admitted openly that so far as the position of exciseman is concerned, he can appoint any person whether he has passed any examination or not, or whether
he is qualified for the position or not. He can override the Civil Service Act by appointing a deputy collector, and then telling the collector of inland revenue that the deputy collector is to fill the position of excise officer. That is practically the answer the hon. minister has given me. Such being the case, he has certainly been trying to override the Civil Service Act in the case of that appointment in the town of Prescott. I am glad to get his answer so fully and clearly, because it is evident that when it is really the wish of the minister to override the Civil Service Act, he can do so. I know that a great many people have been seeking positions in the department, and when I have told them that the minister could override the Act if he wished, and could appoint any one he chose, they would hardly believe it. But the minister owns that in this case he did get round the Act. AVlien other vacancies occur, I hope he will not overlook the claims of other people by holding up the Civil Service Act as an obstacle, because he knows that for any position in the Inland Revenue Department it is mot necessary for a candidate to pass the Civil Service Act, but that it is simply a dead letter so far as that department is concerned.

1 am glad to have heard the criticism of my hon. friend. It might perhaps be proper to change the law ; but I must tell the hon. gentleman that I have acted in accordance with the law. If I have done wrong, I have not been the first to do so. I have followed the example of my predecessors under the old regime and under the present regime. I have made no new departure in this case. If I had the time I might give a long list of those who have been appointed deputy collectors during the past twenty-five years or since the law was enacted. My hon. friend would hardly, I think, be satisfied to justify his way of conducting the department by referring to his predecessors. Mr. ItEID (Grenville). I beg pardon. The hon. minister Las admitted on the floor of the House, that, so far as the Inland Revenue Department is concerned, it is not necessary for any man to pass any examination whatever in order to fill any position in the department. He explains that if he wants to fill any position in his department-exciseman or sorter or anything else-all he has to do is simply to appoint a man a deputy collector and tell the .collector to assign to him the duties of an exciseman. In that way he can override the Civil Service Act and'make it a dead letter. I think this should be thoroughly understood by people from one end of the Dominion to the other, so that when vacancies occur, everybody may know whether it is necessary to pass an examination or not. Am I not right in that ?

I think my hon. friend is going a little too far. What he says is a fact, that the position of deputy collector is open under the law, which has been in force for twenty-five years, and through that door, we might fill all the positions in the department; but that is not my fault, it is the law. Of course, if that were unduly taken advantage of, there would be an end of the Civil Service Act, but I am not aware that any undue advantage has been taken of this provision. The law was passed some twenty years ago and under it a certain number of deputy collectors were appointed, but 1 think that the hon. gentleman is gojng too far when he says that the law has been abused. It certainly has not been abused by me. I have always been apxious that those desirous of entering the service should pd"ss the qualifying examination. There was no abuse of the law in Prescott. That is a large division and there were two deputy collectors there. In that town there are. a distillery and a brewery, and when one of the positions became vacant, Mr. White was appointed a deputy collector, without passing any qualifying examination. If the law allows deputy collectors to be appointed without passing any examination, I cannot be blamed, and it is the duty of any member of parliament who objects to this, to move to amend the law.

The hon. minister admits what I [DOT] have said, namely, that through the appointment of deputy collectors without examination, he can fill every position in the Inland Revenue Department. Am 1 right ?
No, you are not right there.

I would like to understand if I am right when I say that the- minister could first appoint a man a deputy collector, although he had not passed the qualifying examination, and then that Mr. HEYD.
man could be detailed to fill any other position, whether exciseman or any other.

I have already explained that after a man is appointed a deputy collector, his duties are assigned to him'by the collector. If the collector finds that he is qualified to fulfil the duties of accountant, he may give him those duties to fulfil. If he finds that he is competent to fill the position of' exciseman, he can give him that position, but that does not mean that from the moment the position of deputy collector is opeued, every person can be admitted into the service through that door. That has never been done to my knowledge. We have appointed temporary officers pending their examination, and after they have passed their examination, we have made them excisemen, but the duties to be performed by each and every officer are assigned to him by the collector.

The hon. minister throws the whole responsibility on the collector. When this position of exciseman became vacant in the town of Prescott, it required a man with certain qualifications to fill it. If the man appointed to fill that vacancy had not the necessary qualifications, then the hon. minister should be man enough to take the-responsibility, but he shelters himself behind his collector. But surely, if, when the position of exciseman became vacant in the town of Prescott, the hon. minister appointed a man as deputy collector, and that man was then assigned to the position of exciseman, the responsibility must fall on the hon. gentleman, and he should own up that it is he, and not the collector, who is responsible. The hon. minister says that such has been the law for the last twenty years, and he is not responsible, but he is there to see that the spirit and the intention of the law are carried out, and I believe that if we had the debates in the House when this Civil Service Act was passed, it would show that the understanding was that certain qualifications should be required of an exciseman. A customs officer in charge of a distillery requires certain qualifications. He must have sufficient education to enable him to pass the qualifying examination, and I find it strange that the Auditor General would pay the wages of a man who was appointed to fill the position of exciseman in a distillery, and who had not passed the qualifying examination. Take the case of Mr. White, the hon. minister appointed him a deputy collector and then he was put in the position of exciseman in a distillery or brewery, although he had not passed that qualifying examination which is required of excisemen. Let this practice be followed, and you could fill the Inland Revenue service with men who had not passed the quali-

fying examination, but who had siinp!y been appointed deputy collectors and then assigned to fill other positions.
