To enable the department to supply methylated spirits to manufacturers, the cost of which will be recouped by the manufacturers to whom it is supplied, and to pay for rent, light, power, freight, salaries. &c., $60,000.
Has that contract with the Standard Chemical Company been renewed, and, if so, for how long ?

1 explained to the House some time ago how it happened that this contract was made in 1898. In order to give the committee an opportunity to learn everything in connection with the contract, I will give all the explanation that can be obtained in "the records of the department. This sum of $G0,000 is to enable the department to purchase alcohol and wood naphtha for the manufacture of methylated spirits to supply manufacturers, and to pay for rent, light, power, freight, salaries, &c. The amount expended in the last fiscal year was $52,017.01.
The manufacture of methylated spirits was taken over from the bonded manufacturers and carried on by the department as a protection to the revenue on July 1, 1888. It was known that methylated spirits was being used as a substitute for genuine potable spirits, which was objectionable not only from a revenue standpoint, but also ! on the ground of injury to the public health. It was thus deemed necessary to take sole control of this manufacture and to supply it to responsible persons for stated purposes. Two grades were established : No. 1, consisting of about 25 per cent of wood naphtha, and No. 2, consisting of about 50 per cent. Grade No. 1 is supplied to varnish and other manufacturers who have obtained the necessary permit from the department,- and have entered into bond, with sureties in the sum of $2,000, that such spirits shall only be used for the purposes mentioned and on the premises described in their application. The present price of this grade is $1.10 per gallon. It is used in the manufacture of varnish, liquid'glue, leather dressing, stove and shoe polish, &e. Grade No. 2 is supplied to the trade for burning and other purposes without the issue of a permit and without entering into bonds. This is due to the fact that the percentage of wood naphtha is so large that its use for potable purposes would be impossible. The present price is $1.50 per gallon. The reason for the price of the latter being higher than the better grade is the large quantity of wood naphtha used, which costs the department $1.40 per gallon as against 42 cents per gallon paid for alcohol. The quantity of both grades sold during the fiscal year ending June 30, 1902, was 52,835 standard gallons, and the balance of receipts over expenditure amounted to $23,755.47.

I was asked some time ago to give particulars with regard to the contract entered into between the department and the company. Here is a copy of the contract which was passed between the department and the Standard Chemical Company. I will read the document.

Never mind reading it. If the minister will let us see the contract, there is no necessity for reading it.
The MINISTER OF INLAND REVENUE, (reading.)
The contract was made between the Rathbun Company of Deseronto. in the province of Ontario. a body corporate and politic, of the first part, and the Standard Chemical Company of Toronto, in the said province, a body corporate and politic, of the second part, the said two companies being hereafter referred to together as the said companies ; and Her Majesty the Queen, represented by the Minister of Inland Revenue of Canada of the third part.

Does the minister intend to renew the contract 1

No, my intention is to buy from the companies which are in a position to supply a good article. We shall purchase wood naphtha the same as we buy alcohol from the distillers, viz., according to the production.
What is the date of that report ?
[DOT]Tuiy 26, 1S98. The contract was to run five years.
It has taken a long time to answer the very simple question I asked the minister, namely, whether he intended to renew the contract.

I said no. The contract was not renewed, and I do not propose to renew it.
Mr, BENNETT. I congratulate the hon. minister on his backbone in not acceding to the wishes of some of the gentlemen who asked him to renew it. Will tenders be called for the supply of methylated spirits

required by the department during the current year ?

I do not think there are more than two companies which are in a position to supply wood alcohol, and as I do not propose to go to the United States or elsewhere to buy that article, I propose to buy it from the same companies or any other companies at the current prices in the same way as we buy grain alcohol to mix with the wood alcohol at one time from one distiller and at another time from another distiller, according to the quantity he has to sell.

If the kon. minister proposes that we shall be at the mercy of this combine I would suppose that he better try to get this contract renewed at the combination's own price. Is there any private party who permits himself to be at the mercy of any combination in this country ? I think the hon. minister will do well to secure prices from American or European firms, and if this combination which is composed of political friends of lion, gentlemen opposite are not prepared to sell this article at an honest living price, let outsiders have the benefit of the contract. The hon. minister raised the duty on this article from $2 to $2.40 a gallon. It will be a source of great satisfaction to the genera! public to know that the hon. minister, instead of renewing the contract, proposes to place himself within the grasp of this combination. .
I think the hon. gentleman has misunderstood me. I do not know that any other company besides the Rathbun people and the Standard Chemical Company are in a position to supply that article.
They are one and the same. That came out in the debate a few weeks ago.
Yes, they were amalgamated at that time and I think they are still so.
That is right.

Then there is only one company. I am informed that other concerns propose to manufacture the same article and that is the reason why I do not feel inclined to ask for tenders. What would be the use of asking for tenders when there is now only one concern able to supply the article ?
The hon. gentleman will get the benefit of American competition and this would enable him to keep these people within honest prices.

I do not think it would be wise to bring in American competition, but if these gentlemen ask too much for this article we can I 169
go to the United States, as we have done in tlie past, or to Germany, France or elsewhere. The Standard Chemical Company, I understand, have already three or four and perhaps five manufactories in the country, three at least in Ontario, one in Quebec, and I am informed that they are going to start another. This company have never exacted more than the current price. If you take the figures running from 1880 to 18SS you will find that the average price ranged from $1.50 to $1.60 per gallon.
If the hon. minister will permit me I would inform him that the same company are selling the same article in Ottawa to-day for $1.05 per gallon and the department are paying $1.40 a gallon.

Who was appointed to fill the vacancy caused by the appointment of Mr. Keilty to be collector at Prescott ?
There has been no appointment up to the present.

When Mr. White was appointed that made two deputy collectors at Prescott. The hon. minister has been trying to carry out the Civil Service Act and the point I wish to make is that he could appoint any one to fill the position of deputy collector and that one or more deputy collectors could be appointed at the same port. According to the Civil Service Act there should be a collector, a deputy collector, and the balance of the officials at a port should be excisemen. In Perth I find that the hon. minister has one collector and six deputy collectors. Therefore, he is filling the position of excisemen with deputy collectors.

I think my hon. friend is entirely mistaken. Ail these deputy collectors are not stationed at Perth. They represent other localities in the division. I will give the names of these gentlemen and the stations where they- are located. Mr. H. T. Noonan is the deputy collector at Perth; Mr. Thomas Clarke, deputy collector at Pembroke; Mr. W. E.



Rowan, deputy collector at Arnprior; Mr. W. Egan, deputy collector at Renfrew ; Mr. J. George, deputy collector at Eganville. When we have bonded warehouses In a certain locality In a division we place a deputy collector in charge of it. These gentlemen have not passed their examination and they would not likely do so because of the very small salaries that they are in receipt of. Some of tihese salaries are very small. One receives $187. another $53, and another, $269, &c. We appoint a deputy collector at the head office and at each outside place where we have a bonded warehouse to survey.
What difference does it make where he is, if he fills the position of exciseman ?
He is only the keeper of a warehouse in a certain locality, and that it requires no special qualification.
There is this man J. A. Wood, at Prescott. Is he a deputy collector ?
He is a deputy collector at Brockville. He is the brother of the late Controller of Inland Revenue.
Is Prescott the only place where you have two or more deputy collectors ?

Oh, no. We have deputy collectors in class A and class B at Quebec and Montreal, and in fact in every important town we have several deputy collectors. Some of these officers are filling positions in the country districts in the same division. They have the survey of bonded warehouses and they are deputy collectors for the place they are in.
Has the minister any deputy collectors who fill the position of excisemen, the same as in the town of Prescott ?

The duties assigned to the deputy collector are not necessarily those of an exciseman. If a man is specially qualified, the collector would assign him to the duties of exciseman, and perhaps an exciseman may fill the duties of an accountant, if he is qualified. The title is nothing; the collector selected the best men to perform the work.
It appears quite plain from what the minister says, that men are appointed as deputy collectors, but are filling the position that excisemen should fill.

Returning to the wood alcohol question. I suppose the minister knows that wood alcohol is now being sold at a much less price than form-Hon. Mr. BERNIER.
erly. The minister is aware that the price in the United States is much lower than here. Does he know tha price in the United States at the present time ?	.
The last information I have is that it is $1.08 an imperial gallon.

The minister is well aware that until recent years such by-products of wood alcohol as acetic acid and tar had practically little sale in Canada, owing to the introduction of the national policy these by-products have become more valuable and the price of wood alcohol has been reduced. I understand that these wood alcohol concerns sell the stuff to dealers all over the country at a little over $1 a gallon.
I know they are starting new manufactories.
Is this wood alcohol produced by any others except the Rathbun Company and the Standard Chemical Company ?
Not to my knowledge. Some time ago I received a letter from a Sault Ste. Marie company, stating that at some time in the future they would be able to supply a certain quantity of wood alcohol.

When we discussed this matter before, the minister was asked if he would call for public tenders when this contract expired, and now that it is about to expire, I would ask him again if it is his intention to ask for tenders for the supply of this wood alcohol.

I have already given a full explanation with regard to that, but I will explain it again. The contract will expire on the 26th July next, and my intention is not to renew the contract. We will buy wood alcohol as we buy the grain alcohol, at the current price.
But the question is, will you ask for tenders V
No. I could not ask for tenders, and buy from the different producers, because, if one tender was accepted, we would have to buy from that firm only.
We want to make it clear that the Minister of Inland Revenue intends to spend $35,000 of the money of the people for wood alcohol without asking for public tenders.
If I asked for tenders now, who would tender ?
This other firm which the hon. minister speaks of would be in a position to do so.
If there are two this year, and there might be four or five next year, I think it would be better to wait until we have a chance of buying the article at the lowest price.
Who came down and asked that question ?

I think my hon. friend should be satisfied with my answer. I do not want to name any body who came to my department. If the hon. gentleman should come to my office and ask for something, I would not be bound to state in the House that he had been in my office. But some persons who was connected with that firm came to me, and I said 1 would not renew the contract.

I would remind the hon. minister that since the beginning of this session, we had certain discussions about Mr. Fyfe, the chief inspector of weights and measures, in connection witli what several of the members affected, believed to be an insolent reflection cast upon them in a certain report made to the deputy minister 169|
by Mr. Fyfe, about an automatic weighing device in which the grain threshers of Manitoba and the North-west Territories were interested. If I remember aright, I think it was indicated to the minister that those members who believed themselves to be affected by that insolent reference, would expect that at the proper time something in the nature of an apology would be tendered to them by this officer. I beg, therefore, to ask the minister if any steps have been taken by him or by his deputy to procure from Mr. Fyfe such an apology as would be deemed satisfactory to the members affected ?	.

I have no doubt that if Mr. Fyfe, who 1 am sure is a gentleman, thought he had insulted any of these gentlemen from the west, he would be ready to retract and apologize. But I have read the remarks, and l think I have heard here remarks which were a great deal more insulting than the language which he used. Still, I will call tile attention of Mr. Fyfe to the matter, and I think that if he finds that he has insulted any members of the House, or even any citizen in Manitoba or the North-west Territories, he will retract.

Well, I may remark that it is some five or six weeks since this question was discussed in this House, and the matter was brought to the attention of the minister, and I suppose that Mr. Fyfe's attention must also have been drawn to it ; and I have not yet had any intimation from any person that Mr. Fyfe had in contemplation any manner of apology for this reference. As there may be members here who are not aware of the reference made by this gentleman in an official report to members of this House, it may be well for me to place the matter again before this committee.
How came this statement to be made ?

Two years ago, and one year ago, and again this year, members on both sides of the House, from Manitoba and the North-west Territories, spoke of a certain automatic weighing device which tlie grain threshers of the western country have found it absolutely necessary t.o use, but which, up to the time of this session, tiie Department of Inland Revenue had refused to verify. It was, therefore, being used illegally. The result was that the threshers were not able legally to collect tlieir accounts, but had to depend on the honour of the various individuals for whom they did work. The members from Manitoba and the North-west, a year ago were asked to go over to the Department of Inland Revenue to witness a test of this machine. The test was, I may say, absolutely satisfactory to all of us, and we

understood at the time that it was satisfactory to the officers of the department. As a matter of fact the proper officer of the department, whose duty it was to adjudicate on the matter, was satisfied with it, and was willing to verify it; and, according to a document which was in the possession of the hon. member for Selkirk (Mr. McCreary) when we were discussing this matter before, it appears that that officer did verify it, or, on his recommendation, it was verified according to law. It was explained by the minister that this officer was simply acting, not having been regularly appointed. Later, another appointment was made, that of Mr. Fyfe, who I understand was brought from Montreal, and he cancelled the recommendation of the gentleman who had been filling the office. The question was brought before the House again this session, by my hon. friend from Lisgar (Mr. Stewart), but in the meantime, there had beeu considerable correspondence going on between the owners of the patent and the officers of the department, and this correspondence was brought down in a return moved for by the hon. member for Lisgar. This return includes a report made by Mr. Fyfe, one of the paragraphs of which I shall read to the House :
The members who are fighting that battle for the ' grain threshing scale ' makers, do not seem to see that they are unknowingly occupying a false position.
Here is an officer of the department who says that members of this House are occupying a false position.
Opposed to their own interests.
Those western members are, in the opinion of this officer, fools. I do not know that we can complain of his opinion, but we can complain of his expressing it officially in a report.
Is he a western man ?

No, he is a Montreal man.
Opposed to their own interests and the interests of those they represent ? They have within reach an article that will meet the requirements of the law, which can be made by any manufacturer without royalty, and yet they are trying to force upon the farmers of the west an inferior machine that is patented and is the exclusive property of one manufacturer.
This is a reflection upon myself and colleagues, which may or may not be true, but at all events it is not the business of any subordinate officer of this department to make any such reflection, and I think that before we vote this salary, we should have the assurance that proper apologies will be made by him.

1 have toid my hon. friend thai there might perhaps be a difference of opinion with regard to the application of the sentence he has just read, but I am convinced .that if Mr. Fyfe is made aware that, in the 'opinion Mr. SCOTT.
of certain members, he has been guilty of a want of courtesy or has expressed an opinion which might be construed by hon. gentlemen, who have a proper regard for their own dignity, as a reflection or an insult, he would be the first to apologize, for I have known Mr. Fyfe many years and have always known him to be a gentleman.
Has their been an increase to his salary ?
No, he was appointed at the maximum, $2,500, and there is no increase.
His salary should. be decreased until he qualifies himself for the business. He is ignorant of the conditions and requirements of the west.

The members from Manitoba and the North-west thoroughly understood the position they occupied and what they had to do in order to get relief for the men who were doing $5,000,000 worth of work for which they could not collect a cent; and if we were led into any misunderstanding with ragard to that particular machine, it was the fault of the hon. minister and his officers who invited us to examine it. It was not due to any act on our part, but on the part of the hon. minister himself, and I consider that both the hon. gentleman and his deputy acquiesced in the remarks of Mr. Fyfe when they permitted such a report to pass through their hands and come down to this House. It is all very well for the minister and his deputy to sit here at Ottawa and make no move to enable threshing machine owners to collect the $5,000,000 worth of work above referred to, but when the members from the west endeavoured to have the machine which the minister and his deputy suggested would meet the requirements, tljis is the way in which this officer sees fit toNwefer to them. I claim that these members have a very strong case against this man, and this item should stand until we hear what he has to say with regard to the remarks he has made.
Is the hon. minister willing that the item should stand until we have some satisfaction ?	,
I have already explained to my hon. friend that if he is convinced that this sentence of Mr. Fyfe conveys an insult, Mr. Fyfe will be the first to retract.
Might I ask the hon. gentleman has an explanation of this statement ever been asked for from Mr. Fyfe ?
Never.
Is the hon. minister satisfied that the statement should go as it is ?

These hon. gentlemen are taking a new de-

parture. To reimburse E. Forrest, cashier of the Montreal Inland Revenue office, for moneys abstracted from his cash drawer and which he was called upon to make good, $85.

During the year 1900 and prior thereto the cashier of the Montreal office suffered the purloining of a sum of money from the cash drawer. To pay assistant inspector M. J. Kelly of Quebec, amount withheld by Inspector Bourassa, $159.90.

The services of Mr. Bourassa, the inspector were dispensed with in November, 1896, and some time after, the department was advised that he had not paid the account of his assistant inspector, Mr. Kelly, for June and July, 1896. The department having paid the sum to the inspector, it was unable to pay it again to the assistant inspector. It is thought only just that the department should pay this amount to Mr. Kelly. Mr. Bourassa promised to pay it, provided the government would repay him what he had contributed to the superannuation fund, but as he had been dismissed for withholding the collections of the department, the refund could not be made. Might I ask the minister whether the duties of these electric light inspectors go beyond the inspection of meters ? Have they anything to do with the inspection of machinery or parts of machinery or any part of the electric light plant, and more particularly 'transformers ?
4The MINISTER OF INLAND REVENUE.
No, they have only to inspect the meters.

Well, I think some government in Canada, either the federal or the local, should supervise in some way these electric light plants all over the Dominion. I happened to be concerned in an electric light arbitration last winter, and in the course of the evidence it came out that owing to defective transformers a number of live* had been lost. Owing to defects in the different parts of the electric light plant, deaths have occurred. I think that these were attributable to the fact that the transformers, which regulate the power, had become practically worn out. There was one case in Ottawa where a man went to

the stable to turn on the electric light and his dead body was found there. The department should undertake to have a rigid inspection of electric light plants wherever established.

For fourteen years and a half we had an inspector of inland revenue in the province of Nova Scotia, but now we have none, and the work is being done by a man from St. John, New Brunswick. I am afraid to say anything about St. John after what I said the other night, but I have reason to believe that he is not very acceptable to those who are in the service of the Inland Revenue Department for the province of Nova Scotia, and a memorial signed by the members from Nova Scotia supporting the government has been sent in asking the hon. minister to provide the necessary sum in the supplemen-taries, so that we may have a proper officer appointed as inspector of Inland Revenue for Nova Scotia. Surely when we had one during fourteen years, we ought to have one now when our population has increased and there is greater necessity for his services.
This matter is under consideration.
Has the inspection of electric light plants ever been- brought to the hon. gentleman's notice.

Never. Under the law, the powers of the inspectors of electric lights are very limited. It would be very important that some inspection should be made of this plant, but this would require the services of a more competent man, a mechanical man of experience, and I do not know if, under the provision of the local law, there is not some inspection of these establishments provided - for. Our inspector of electric lights would have no right to visit the plant.
The services of one man would do for the province of Ontario because the inspection of one plant once a year would suffice.
Would not that come under the Provincial Factory Act V

I hardly know whether it would be the duty of the province to see to that or not, but it would be money well spent by the Dominion if a good man were appointed, say in Ontario. I think a good man could be secured at a salary of $1,500, who might go from one town to another and inspect the plant, whether owned by a municipality or a company. We have had three or four deaths in Ontario caused by a live wire. There was one in Ottawa and one in the town of Chesley. Owing to the defects in the transformers, or to their being worn out, so great a volume of power came 170
over the wire that simply to touch it killed a man.

I am not very familiar with the duties of electric light inspectors, but judging by the description given by the hon. minister they are rather of a nominal character, and the work that should be done by an electric light inspector is not really done at all. I have never yet discovered the actual benefit conferred on the community by means of the services such as are referred to in the item of $800.
I can understand the testing of meters. Every meter is tested before it goes out, but that would surely occupy a very small portion of the year. The hon. minister is asking us to vote $800 for the salaries of two men-one at Three Rivers and one somewhere else.
One $500 at Three Rivers, and one $300 at St. Hyacinthe.
For the purpose of testing meters at these two places. How many hours a year will these gentlemen be employed ?

I cannot say exactly. I understand that the same men are generally inspectors of gas and electricity. They inspect the gas meters and test the purity of the gas but they do not inspect electric meters except when called upon either by the company or by the one who uses the meter. They cannot touch the instrument except in the presence of the parties.
The law provides for inspection once a year ?
Owing to fires or removals or other accidents, they may be called at any moment to inspect some meters.

Would it not be wise to have them make an inspection once a year of a certain number of meters at least, selected indifferently. Why is it desirable to restrict their inspection to cases where they are called in, because the majority of people are not aware that they have that right to call upon the services of the inspector.
The law requires an inspection every five years.
Why not make it once a year ?

Experience has shown that these meters do not require to be inspected oftener than once in five years. With regard to more frequent inspection, perhaps the users or the company would object. They do not like these instruments to be touched by anyone. When



properly inspected, they are fixed and nobody can touch them except with the consent of both parties, but the services of the inspector might be called upon at any moment on account of fires or removal or other accident so that he must be on the spot and charge a certain amount for the inspection. They have nothing to do with the repairing the meters-that is the affairs of the company. The inspector only waits until his services are called for to examine the meter when the parties disagree.
Of course, the insulation of wires and the adoption of other methods for the protection of life and property are really more important than the purposes which seem to be served by the Act at present.

I admit readily that a more rigid inspection of the installation and of how the wires are fixed would be very important. But, as the law is now, the officers have no duty except to inspect the meters, either gas or electric.

The fire insurance associations in some cities have what they call an inspection of these electric light installations. But, in some places, at least, I do not think the inspection amounts to anything, I know that in some parts of Nova Scotia with which I am more familiar, electric light installations have been made that are really of a dangerous character. I do not say that that is the case now, but I know that it has been the case in the past and it may be so now for all I know to the contrary. It depends, I suppose, to some extent on the person employed to do the work. It seems to me that it would be very desirable that these officers should be given duties, and they should be capable of performing those duties, more nearly concerning the safety of life and property. We know that in various parts of the Dominion men have been killed as the result of improper insulation of wires or through the proximity of telephone or telegraph wires. A telegraph or telephone wire may get broken and come in contact with an electric light wire, and a person passing along the street coming in contact with that wire may be killed. It does not seem to me that the precautions necessary to avoid accidents of that kind are in any way under the control or subject to the inspection of those officers. These matters are of greater importance than the duties performed by these officers at the present time-looking after meters, and, possibly testing the strength of the electric current. The minister might say whether this subject has been under consideration.

The question is a very important one, and I thank the hon. leader of the opposition for having brought it to my attention. I shall carefully examine the law as it stands Hon. Mr. BERNIER.
and see what can be done in the direction he has indicated.
Would not the trouble be that if the government undertook to say when wires were properly placed in a house, if anything resulted prejudicial to the owners, the government would be responsible ?

I do not think it would be right to undertake the inspection of every house, but there might be an inspection with regard to plant and material. But at present the only duty assigned to our officers is to test these meters.

I think they go further than that sometimes, and that they ought to do so. One trouble with the electric light is that a plant for so many lights of say, sixteen candle-power is installed, and the light is not really more than eight candle-power. Who is to determine whether they are up to the standard or not ? The inspector does so when he comes around. There may be no meters in connection with the plant. In our plant there are none. The inspector goes to a store where the consumer has refused to accept the statement of the parties supplying the light, claiming that it is not up to the standard and decides that matter. But the trouble is that the inspectors are not always available. They ought to go round every year and be available at any time, for the light may be up to the standard to-night and very defective to-morrow night-it depends on how the dynamo is run and how many volts go through. That cannot be determined by the user of the light and he must depend on somebody else.
Adulteration of food-to pay Mr. J. M. Ferguson. barrister of Montreal, for professional services in connection with the preparation and drafting of amended Act 61 Vic. chapter 24. $100.

I suppose my hon friends of the legal profession will have no objection to passing this item. Mr. Ferguson was engaged foh this work in 1898, he having special qualifications in his knowledge of the law with respect to the adulteration of food. He was selected by the minister at that time, Sir Henri Joly de Lotbiniere. I suppose these expenses should have been borne by the Department of Justice. The claim has been a long time pending. Fnally the case was submitted to the department of the Minister of Justice, and that department found that $100 was a fair and reasonable payment for these services. The drafting of the law called for the services of a member of the legal profession.
Why could not a law clerk draft it ?
I think a great deal too much outside assistance has been procured for such purposes as this.
This is the only case in my department.

I am not speaking of this department alone. We had a reference the other day to the very large sum paid for drafting the Railway Commission Bill now before the House. I am not going to say at present that there is not some justification for going outside occasionally. There may have been circumstances which made it necessary to do so in the case of the Railway Commission Bill. But I think there are men in the Department of Justice who are just as capable of drafting this Bill as the gentleman in Montreal, who was selected to do this work. We have a Department of Justice, with a very large staff, and I would like to know why a small Bill of this kind should not be sent to the Department of Justice, and prepared there instead of being sent to Montreal. There are officers in the Inland Revenue Department who know what is wanted, surely, and there is a properly organized Department of Justice with a large staff, and these gentlemen are left to employ their time as best they can, while the drafting of this measure is sent to Montreal. I regard a course of that kind and absolutely unjustifiable. I believe that if we had an inquiry made of the Deputy Minister of Justice and his assistants, not one of them would dare to say that this Bill could not have been prepared in the Department of Justice without overworking any man in that department. Under these circumstances I absolutely protest against work of this kind being sent out, when we have not only a Department of Justice, but a law clerk, and some times two or three in nearly every department of this government.
We have none in our department.

In nearly every department. I think there are two in the Railway Department. I am not finding any fault with that. But I am finding fault, when we have this enormous staff of lawyers in the public service, with paying men in the legal profession for work which could just as well have been done by the regular employees of this government.
